finding: The live range of $100-$700 is about right for what most drivers are quoted (one failed coil, or a full set on a four-cylinder), but the top is too low for a full set of genuine coils on a six- or eight-cylinder engine. Built totals for a FULL SET (coils for every cylinder + stated hours x $120-$160 per hour, the national middle rate used for this arithmetic): economy 2017 Kia Forte 2.0L, 4 coils, $182-$416; midsize 2017 Honda CR-V 1.5L turbo, 4 coils, $278-$430; truck 2016 Ford F-150 5.0L V8, 8 coils, $280-$929; luxury 2013 BMW 335i, 6 coils, $355-$833. Across the four that is roughly $180-$930. For ONE COIL the parts cost seen is $44.95-$79.98 (Forte), $60.38-$87.50 (CR-V, genuine only), $58.19-$96.18 (F-150, genuine only) and $19.19-$85.50 (335i). No source states a separate single-coil labor time for any of these four vehicles (Ford and GM print one-coil times for other vehicles, given below); using the full-set time as a ceiling, one coil comes to about $117-$176 on the Forte, $96-$168 on the CR-V, $118-$256 on the F-150 and $259-$406 on the BMW (the BMW figure is dominated by a two-hour do-it-yourself ceiling and is probably overstated). So the $100 floor fits a single coil on an easy four-cylinder, and $700 covers every one-coil job and every four-cylinder full set we could build; a full set of Ford-list coils on the V8 ($929) or genuine BMW coils on the six ($833) goes past it. The outside estimates agree on the shape: RepairPal $238-$320, Jerry $142-$234 for one coil, J.D. Power $150-$350 for one coil and $300-$800 or more for coil-on-plug systems, YourMechanic examples $295-$829. If the live range is meant to cover a full set on larger engines, a top near $900-$950 is supportable; if it is meant as a one-coil price, $700 is generous. How solid the labor times are: the Forte time is a manufacturer warranty time for this exact job on this exact car (0.6 hour for all four), the best figure here, though warranty times run short. The CR-V time is not a coil operation: it is Honda's warranty time for changing the four spark plugs, which requires taking all four coils off and refitting them. The F-150 range is now three statements from one parts seller for this exact engine, 'approx 30 minutes' for one eight-coil set and 'approx 1 hour' for two others: specific to the truck, but a seller's approximation and not a flat-rate time. The BMW time is now tied to the N55 engine: a parts seller's guide naming the 2011-2015 335i says the spark plug job, which means pulling each coil, takes a home mechanic 'around 2 hours', matching the same seller's general 'under 2 hours' for coils; it is still a do-it-yourself figure for a neighbouring job and probably overstates shop time. Manufacturer times found for other vehicles, shown for scale and not used in the ranges: Ford TSB 26-2210 allows 0.3-0.8 hour for one coil and 0.5-1.0 hour for two or more on 2024-2025 four-cylinder models (2024 Ranger 2.3L 0.6 and 0.8; 2024-2025 Explorer 2.3L 0.4 and 0.6; 2024-2025 Lincoln Corsair 2.0L 0.8 and 1.0), each including reading the codes; GM bulletin PIP6073 allows 0.5 hour to swap-test and replace one coil on a 2025 Silverado 1500 V8; Hyundai TSB 20-FL-001H allows 0.7 hour for one or two coils and 0.8 hour for three or four on the 2017 Elantra 2.0L, including a code check and software update. These sit in the same 0.3 to 1 hour band as the times used for the Forte, CR-V and F-150, which makes the BMW's 2 hours the outlier. Confidence stays low because only the Forte has a manufacturer time for the coil job itself: the CR-V and BMW times are for the spark plug job on the same engine, and the F-150 times are a seller's approximations. Caveats on parts: no aftermarket coil for the CR-V 1.5L was found, so its low end is the genuine coil at a discounted online price; no single aftermarket coil price was loaded for the F-150; no BMW dealer list price was loaded, so the BMW high end is the dearest genuine price seen at a parts seller; the dealer-catalog prices are listed per coil without the word 'each' and were multiplied by the number of cylinders. Not covered: engines where the intake manifold must come off to reach the rear coils (many transverse V6s), and older engines with a single coil pack and plug wires.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee, since most visits start with a misfire or check engine light and the shop has to confirm which coil has failed. Spark plugs are commonly replaced at the same time (the coils are already off), and coil boots if they are cracked or oil-soaked. A valve cover gasket may be added if oil is found in the plug wells, and an intake manifold gasket on engines where the manifold comes off to reach the rear coils. Shops often recommend replacing all coils when one fails on a high-mileage engine, which multiplies the parts cost by the number of cylinders. Shop supplies and sales tax are extra. A misfire that has been driven on for a long time can damage the catalytic converter, which is a separate and much larger repair.
